items.title: Player interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2012
items.q: I mean that was the big thing for Louis Armstrong. Because he had a mixed band they didn’t want him playing in New Orleans, where he was from

ctx.x: Well you know, sometimes I think in jazz or in a lot of fields it’s easier to write about things that are negative or that need to be fixed. And recently I’ve been reading articles about jazz and race, jazz and gender, jazz and generations. Is there any issues with that in the current New Orleans music scene?

Oh in the current music scenes? I mean, I don’t really feel that way a lot. I think that we still have racism in our country, and I think maybe for some people, you know, that’s the case. But as far as it being the way it was in the 50’s or the 40’s, you know, I mean musicians play together now, it doesn’t matter you color, if you’re male or female, you know, it’s just about being together and making music. I think there were times when there were laws that would not allow the musicians to play together. I mean…
and that’s all that matters to us. So I don’t know, I guess that’s different for different people.
